app.title: nerdz
app.subtitle: Decode like a robot.
stage.qr.0.title: Structure
stage.qr.0.label: Structure
stage.qr.0.short: Every QR code has three big corner squares and timing strips. Those help the scanner find the code from any angle.
stage.qr.1.title: Format & Mask
stage.qr.1.label: Format
stage.qr.1.short: First the format bits are read, then a pattern is peeled away to reveal the real data hiding underneath.
stage.qr.2.title: Data Reading
stage.qr.2.label: Data
stage.qr.2.short: A reader zig-zags across the code, collecting black-and-white squares into a long string of 1s and 0s.
stage.qr.3.title: Error Correction
stage.qr.3.label: Repair
stage.qr.3.short: Extra repair bits let the code work even when part of it is dirty or damaged.
stage.qr.4.title: Final Decode
stage.qr.4.label: Decode
stage.qr.4.short: Each 8 bits become a letter. Watch the hidden message appear!
fact.qr.0: The three big corner squares are called "finder patterns" — they help a phone find the code even if you hold it sideways!
fact.qr.1: The mask is like a puzzle layer. The scanner XORs it off to reveal the real data hiding underneath.
fact.qr.2: A QR scanner can read about 4,000 characters — that's roughly two whole pages of a book!
fact.qr.3: QR codes can be up to 30% damaged or dirty and still work, thanks to Reed-Solomon math from the 1960s.
fact.qr.4: Each 8 little squares spell one letter using ASCII — the same code computers have used since 1963.
stage.barcode.0.title: Bars & Guards
stage.barcode.0.label: Bars
stage.barcode.0.short: Tall bars rise from left to right. The first and last bars are special "guards" that tell the scanner where the code begins and ends.
stage.barcode.1.title: Width Encoding
stage.barcode.1.label: Widths
stage.barcode.1.short: Each letter is six bars wide. The pattern of thin and thick bars spells out exactly which letter it is.
stage.barcode.2.title: Scanner Sweep
stage.barcode.2.label: Scan
stage.barcode.2.short: A red laser line slides across the bars, reading the pattern of thick and thin like a robot eye.
stage.barcode.3.title: Check Digit
stage.barcode.3.label: Check
stage.barcode.3.short: A special check bar makes sure the scanner read it right. If the math doesn't add up, it tries again.
stage.barcode.4.title: Final Decode
stage.barcode.4.label: Decode
stage.barcode.4.short: Each group of bars resolves to one letter. The hidden message appears, left to right.
fact.barcode.0: Barcodes were invented in 1949 — but the first thing ever scanned in a real store was a pack of Wrigley's chewing gum in 1974!
fact.barcode.1: Code 128 has four bar widths and uses them in patterns of 6 bars to spell out characters. It's like Morse code with rectangles.
fact.barcode.2: A laser scanner doesn't read letters — it just sees bright/dark/bright/dark and measures how long each one is.
fact.barcode.3: The check digit is math magic: if even one bar is read wrong, the calculation fails and the scanner beeps angry.
fact.barcode.4: Barcodes are read in nanoseconds. The slow part is your beeping — that's just so YOU know it worked.
stage.datamatrix.0.title: L-Finder
stage.datamatrix.0.label: L-Finder
stage.datamatrix.0.short: Data Matrix has a big solid "L" along two sides. It helps the scanner find the code even if it's printed on something curved.
stage.datamatrix.1.title: Clock Track
stage.datamatrix.1.label: Clock
stage.datamatrix.1.short: Tiny alternating black-and-white squares along the other two sides tell the scanner exactly how many rows and columns there are.
stage.datamatrix.2.title: Data Region
stage.datamatrix.2.label: Data
stage.datamatrix.2.short: Data is read in a diagonal path through the middle of the grid, filling in 1s and 0s.
stage.datamatrix.3.title: Error Correction
stage.datamatrix.3.label: Repair
stage.datamatrix.3.short: Like QR codes, Data Matrix uses math to fix mistakes. Even damaged codes can usually be read.
stage.datamatrix.4.title: Final Decode
stage.datamatrix.4.label: Decode
stage.datamatrix.4.short: Each 8 bits become a character. The message appears from the grid!
fact.datamatrix.0: Data Matrix codes can be printed smaller than a grain of rice — small enough to laser-mark on a screw!
fact.datamatrix.1: The clock track is like a ruler — it tells the scanner the spacing even if the photo is taken at an angle.
fact.datamatrix.2: NASA uses Data Matrix to track parts on spacecraft because they survive being laser-marked into metal.
fact.datamatrix.3: Data Matrix codes can recover from up to 30% damage, just like QR — but in much less space.
fact.datamatrix.4: Every surgical tool in a modern hospital usually has a tiny Data Matrix marking its serial number.
stage.aztec.0.title: Bullseye Finder
stage.aztec.0.label: Bullseye
stage.aztec.0.short: Aztec codes have a target right in the middle — rings inside rings. Scanners spot the bullseye and lock on instantly.
stage.aztec.1.title: Mode Message
stage.aztec.1.label: Mode
stage.aztec.1.short: The ring around the bullseye is the "map" — it tells the scanner how many layers of data there are.
stage.aztec.2.title: Data Layers
stage.aztec.2.label: Layers
stage.aztec.2.short: Data spirals outward in rings around the bullseye, layer by layer.
stage.aztec.3.title: Error Correction
stage.aztec.3.label: Repair
stage.aztec.3.short: Reed-Solomon math protects the data so the code still works if part of it is messed up.
stage.aztec.4.title: Final Decode
stage.aztec.4.label: Decode
stage.aztec.4.short: Each layer's codewords turn into letters. The message appears, ring by ring.
fact.aztec.0: Aztec codes don't need a "quiet zone" of empty space around them — they can sit right against other ink.
fact.aztec.1: Aztec was invented in 1995 by a man named Andrew Longacre — and named after the look of the bullseye from above.
fact.aztec.2: Most train tickets and airline boarding passes use Aztec codes — because they survive being folded and crumpled.
fact.aztec.3: Aztec codes can repair themselves from up to 95% damage at the highest setting — almost magic.
fact.aztec.4: Some countries put Aztec codes on driver's licenses and ID cards because they're hard to fake.
